6000: On February 24, 2022 Panama’s President, Laurentino Cortizo, signed Law 287, “that recognizes the rights of Nature and the obligations of the state related to these rights”. This signifies a shift to a proactive conservation approach, recognizing the intrinsic worth and inherent Rights of Nature, while offering an opportunity to fulfill gaps in national legislation. By extension, this law recognizes the rights of Sharks and their habitats. This talk analyzes the threats depleting Shark populations while presenting ample evidence to justify enhanced conservation to sustain the ecological role of this species. Panama, one of the most biodiverse countries worldwide, was selected as a case study due to the country’s demonstrated efforts to environmental conservation, including the country’s legal recognition of the Rights of Nature (having now been enacted in law and policy in more than thirty-five countries worldwide), as well as the observed high presence of industrial and artisanal fishing that threatens several species with extinction. This case can act as a microcosm of the conflicting economic interests that prevent enhancing Shark protection, while highlighting imaginative opportunities for holistic, rights-based and equitable solutions. For example, opportunities will be explored to implement Law 287 through supplementary conservation policy based upon best available science to conserve and restore Sharks, thereby helping safeguard the capacity of marine sustenance, coastal economies, and the future health of the Ocean against climate impacts, and in fact, to help retain the country’s very name meaning—“abundance of fish”.
6001: Global demand for shark products continues to drive overexploitation in many nations. Understanding the trade and consumption of shark-derived products is currently dominated by literature focusing on shark fins while markets for shark meat on global, regional, and domestic scales remain poorly understood. However, the trade in shark meat continues to surpass fins contributing to food security and livelihoods in many coastal areas of the world. To understand the global trade in shark meat and the fisheries supplying these markets, it is crucial to build baselines for catch and consumption at national scales. We investigate one important supply chain in Central America, which is predominantly driven by the demand for shark meat. Shark meat is infrequently consumed in Belize yet shark fishing occurs there to supply an export market in neighbouring Guatemala, where seasonal demand for shark meat peaks during the Catholic Lenten season. We disaggregated landings and trade data in Belize to the species level using multiple approaches and found trade from Belize to Guatemala involves at least 19 shark species, including several listed on the Convention on International Trade of Endangered Species (CITES). We will present species-specific baselines for production and consumption in both nations based on DNA barcoding of markets. This information will bridge critical knowledge gaps in understanding the regional dynamics of shark meat trade in Central America. Understanding this trade network has implications for the management of domestic fisheries in these nations, the implementation of international trade regulations, and the conservation of species supplying this demand.
6002: Shark conservation is being hampered by increased fishing pressure and regulatory shortcomings in many regions, resulting in population losses for several species. A growing market for high-value shark fins, has fueled much of the demand for shark products since the 1990s. National and international policy has tried to end the wasteful practice of shark finning by requiring sharks to be landed whole and with their fins naturally attached (FNA), or even prohibiting shark fishing entirely in so-called shark sanctuaries. This study examines anti-finning regulations across 278 exclusive economic zones (EEZs) and four regional fisheries management organizations (RFMOs). Results show that as of 2020 only 36.7% (n=102) of EEZs were covered by a FNA ban and only around 10% (n=28) of EEZs had a complete ban on shark fishing. Some of the largest shark fishing countries (e.g., Pakistan, Iran) had weak legislation. Thirteen expert interviews were undertaken to contextualize and cross-reference these analyses. Over the last two decades, all respondents indicated a declining (n=11) or constant (n=2) trend in shark finning, with rising use of whole sharks and growing markets for shark meat and other goods. Overall, these findings point to places where existing procedures should be strengthened and present regulations can be improved to reduce shark finning and, eventually, shark mortality, at both the RFMO and national levels.

6003: Anthropogenic activities, including exploitative fishing to harvest shark liver oil for cosmetic use, pose a significant threat to sharks. While trade records and routes for shark fins and meat are relatively well documented, little is known about the use and distribution of other commodities like shark liver oil. We do know shark liver oil is the richest natural source for squalene, that the squalene market was valued at $129 million USD in 2020, and that the cosmetic industry is squalene’s principal end use market. Endpoint market monitoring is crucial for improving our understanding of the shark trade, and tracking compliance with trade laws and sourcing policies. Carbon ratio analysis of δ 13 C using gas chromatography - combustion - isotope ratio mass spectrometry (GC-C-IRMS) has been shown to successfully determine squalene’s source even in finished cosmetic samples of mixed squalene origin. A 2015 study used this method to test skin creams, and found that 20% contained shark squalene. Here we complete a broader investigation of squalane’s use and composition in different types of cosmetic products. Using GC-C-IRMS, we found shark squalene in 26% of cosmetic samples, and in 31% of these cases, squalene was of a mixed plant/shark origin. Half of the top 20 global beauty brands contain shark squalane, 89% of products containing shark squalene identify as cruelty-free, and 37% identify as vegan. This research points to the urgent need for species-specific analysis of the shark squalene in trade, and greater transparency and oversight in the cosmetic industry.
6004: The oceanic whitetip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus) was described historically as one of the most abundant pelagic shark species in tropical seas worldwide. Currently, the species is classified as Critically Endangered under the IUCN Red List and listed as threatened globally under the U.S. Endangered Species Act due to significant population declines and threats of overfishing and the international shark fin trade. In the Western and Central Pacific, the species has declined by more than 90% since 1995, with bycatch-related mortality in pelagic longlines representing the most significant source of mortality. In efforts to conserve the oceanic whitetip shark in U.S. Pacific waters, NOAA Fisheries has taken targeted steps under domestic authorities to end overfishing and recover the species. These steps include developing a draft recovery plan highlighting necessary recovery actions for the Western and Central Pacific population. It also includes developing regulations and international recommendations to end overfishing, including an industry-led initiative to require a gear change in Hawaii’s pelagic longline fishery from wire leaders to monofilament and minimize trailing gear to increase survivorship of hooked oceanic whitetip sharks. While these efforts are expected to help end overfishing and contribute to the recovery of oceanic whitetip sharks in the region, the species is highly migratory, occurs in the waters of 50+ countries, and is caught incidentally in numerous fisheries throughout the region, with the United States representing only ~5% of the total catch. Therefore, international collaboration will be critical to successfully conserving the oceanic whitetip shark beyond U.S. waters.

6005: Understanding the trade in shark and ray meat is challenging given the overall lack of data, with uncertainty surrounding total volume and species composition of catches, domestic consumption, imports, and exports. Additionally, marketing of shark and ray meat under different or broad generic names (e.g., cação, arraia) distorts fisheries statistics and consumer transparency. This challenge is particularly acute in Brazil, a top fishing nation and the largest importer of shark and ray meat in the world, resulting in high production and demand, as well as diverse and widespread markets, both national and international. Recognizing Brazil’s major role in the meat trade and the potentially increasing threats to shark and ray populations, the primary focus of this study is to uncover the shark and ray meat trade along the coast of Brazil. We conduct surveys at important landing sites for sharks and rays, fish markets, and supermarkets across 10 coastal states. Various methods are applied for data collection, such as photographs, samples of biological material for DNA sequencing, and interviews with stakeholders. This information is critical for a comprehensive understanding of the use of shark and ray meat for livelihoods, and the impacts of catch and trade of shark and ray meat along the Brazilian coast, helping to identify species at potential risk of extinction, contributing to CITES listings, and promoting sustainable fisheries strategies.

6006: Sphyrna tudes is a small-bodied, poorly understood species of hammerhead shark. In 2019 S. tudes was listed as Critically Endangered by the IUCN, with an estimated population reduction of 80% or more across its range in less than 40 years. The rapid decline of S. tudes can be attributed to overfishing, mostly as bycatch in gillnet fisheries targeting the Acoupa weakfish and shrimp trawling, as well as coastal habitat degradation across its limited geographical and depth range. Unfortunately, the distribution of S. tudes has been mistakenly reported over decades, mainly due to errors in species identification or inaccurate species distribution models. Here, we refine S. tudes distribution by cross-validating species distribution models (SDMs) with a comprehensive literature review and individual record checking, and assess its spatial extinction risk through Bayesian Additive Regression Trees (BART). Our SDM results demonstrate that, while suitable habitat extends from southeastern Brazil to the Gulf of Mexico, the most important region in the world for this species is likely to be Northern South America. Given that suitable habitat is constrained to coastal areas and dissolved oxygen was the most important variable for the SDMs, we employed the BART with two possible scenarios: (1) fishing pressure reduced to zero and (2) mangrove areas increased by 100%. Our analyses demonstrate that S. tudes has a smaller suitable range than previously considered with intensive fishing pressure, and its capture in fisheries need to significantly decrease to avoid extinction.

6007: Over the last two decades there has been an effort to unveil community patterns of elasmobranch cestodes at a macroecological scale, but analyses at infracommunity level are still scarce. In this work the helminth community parasitizing 37 blue sharks (Prionace glauca), both juveniles and adults, is described and compared with previous studies, performing a global assessment of the relative role of the ecological and evolutionary factors in structuring their local tapeworm assemblages. Shark came from two different non previously surveyed regions: Northeast Atlantic (Galicia, Spain) and Western Mediterranean (Valencia, Spain). Helminths from nine different taxa were identified, of which four presented adult specimens and have already been describe infecting blue sharks: Platybothrium auriculatum, Prosobothrium armigerum, Anthobothrium caseyi and Molicola horridus. The five other taxa could not be identified at species level because of their poor condition. All six previous studies providing infracommunity data about blue sharks encountered a group of four cestode species, thus described here as the ‘core’ community parasitizing blue sharks worldwide. Other cestode infections in blue sharks are discussed and a checklist of adult cestodes infecting the spiral valve of blue sharks is provided. At a global geographic scale, tapeworm communities of blue sharks were composed by 10 cestode taxa, 7 of which are exclusive to this host species and share two fundamental traits: their cosmopolitan distribution and their belonging to cestode genera that typically infects carcharhinids. Showing that the influence of ecological factors upon their tapeworm communities is highly constrained by a strong host specificity.
6008: Describing temporal patterns of space use for migratory marine species can provide insights into the biology and ecology of these animals including their role in ecosystem function. Identifying potential triggers for migration, over multi-year time scales can provide a deeper understanding of the physiological and ecological underpinnings of behavior. To examine migration timing and identify biotic and abiotic factors associated with migratory behavior in white sharks in the WNA, we used data from 65 sharks tagged with a combination of satellite and acoustic tags. Tag-based horizontal and vertical movement data from 2012-2022 were used to discern temporal patterns of space use for individual sharks. Dates of departure from and arrival to residency areas were compared to a number of environmental factors (e.g. absolute temperature, delta temperature over time, photoperiod, moon phase) to determine their influence on migration timing. While there was substantial individual variability in migratory routes and timing, abiotic factors including temperature appear to be significant drivers of departure timing from residency areas. Ongoing analyses are exploring the presence and scale of intra-annual variability among individuals along with inter-annual variability within individuals tracked for longer than one year. By providing information on multiple individuals over a broad spatiotemporal scale, these findings provide key information to better understand white shark migration and space use in the region. With changing ocean conditions, elucidating the effects of these changes on oceanic predators and their migratory behavior will be critical to understanding the comprehensive impacts to marine ecosystems.

6009: The oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris) is a circumglobally distributed species, but little to no information exists for many parts of their range. The eastern Atlantic Ocean is a particularly data-deficient area, where manta ray presence has seldom been reported and no description of the distribution, movement, and connectivity of populations within the region exists. This study makes use of satellite telemetry conducted in Cabo Verde, coupled with ecological niche modelling, to provide the first description of an oceanic manta ray population in the eastern Atlantic ocean and the most likely distribution of the species in this region. Repeated surveys between 2015 and 2019 and data from 11 satellite-tracked individuals revealed a reliable and continued presence of manta rays in the archipelago, although the number of sightings was considerably lower than those reported for some of the major aggregation sites for the species and no individual was ever re-sighted. Ecological niche modelling suggests connections between the Gulf of Guinea and Cabo Verde, and revealed stable pockets of habitat within Cabo Verde. The role of Cabo Verde in the life-history of oceanic manta rays in the region remains to be elucidated, though the low abundance and re-sighting frequency, coupled with modelling suggesting seasonal expansion and contraction of suitable habitat, suggests that Cabo Verde might be a key stop-over on a potentially longer movement corridor along the eastern Atlantic Ocean.
6010: The oceanic whitetip shark (Carcharhinus longimanus) is a globally distributed, highly migratory, pelagic shark species that was once considered one of the most abundant sharks in tropical seas globally. Due to significant population declines resulting from threats of overfishing and the international shark fin trade, the oceanic whitetip shark was listed as threatened throughout its range under the U.S. Endangered Species Act (ESA) in January 2018. As required by the ESA, the U.S. National Marine Fisheries Service (NOAA Fisheries) is developing a draft recovery plan for the oceanic whitetip shark that serves as a roadmap to recovery and outlines the path and tasks needed to restore the species to the point where it no longer requires the protections of the ESA. The draft recovery plan identifies both demographic and threats-based criteria to ensure population viability and reduction of threats to the species, as well as comprehensive management, research, and outreach actions needed to successfully reach those criteria. While NOAA Fisheries has the responsibility to develop recovery plans, successful implementation of the oceanic whitetip shark recovery plan will require participation and cooperation from numerous government agencies, stakeholders, international organizations, and non-governmental organizations around the world. This presentation will highlight key elements of the draft recovery plan and opportunities for public and stakeholder involvement in the recovery planning and implementation process.

6011: Sharks were historically abundant throughout oceanic regions; however, today many populations are threatened with extinction. Recent conservation efforts include the creation of large-scale marine protected areas (LMPAs), with a major expectation of LMPAs being the potential to conserve highly migratory species like sharks. In the last 15 years, 17 nations or territories have established ‘shark sanctuaries’, whereby the targeting or retention of sharks is prohibited within territorial waters. Yet, the conservation impacts of such sanctuaries remain unclear. Migratory species may spend limited time in protected areas, and while targeting sharks is prohibited, commercial fishing continues in many sanctuaries. Though sharks caught in sanctuaries are mandated to be released, at-vessel and post-release mortality rates can be significant, particularly in longline fisheries. We combined data from regional fisheries management organizations and satellite remote sensing sources to model longline fishing effort and generate estimates of annual shark catch and mortality in eight Western Pacific shark sanctuaries. We developed a predictive model that estimates the number of longline hooks deployed using satellite-derived vessel positioning data, then generated standardized catch-per-unit-effort rates for 11 species and genera using fisheries observer data and quantified total shark catch. Finally, we predicted total mortality using species-specific at-vessel and post-release mortality rates gleaned from the literature. We find that longline bycatch remains a significant yet undercounted source of mortality for sharks within sanctuaries. Given the data gaps in regional stock assessments for many pelagic species, we discuss the implications of our findings for stock management across the wider fishing region.
6012: Within NE Atlantic waters, the legislative framework in which elasmobranch fisheries operate can be both diverse and complex. Commercial fishers, recreational anglers, processors and fisheries regulators can find the relevant legislation and regulation difficult to interpret and implement. Lack of understanding of such regulations may result in low levels of support within the fishing industry and subsequent reduced levels of compliance, thereby undermining the effectiveness of any management measures. Additionally, species within elasmobranch fisheries can often be similar in appearance and difficult to accurately identify. A history of aggregated landings in some commercial elasmobranch fisheries has also contributed to unreliable catch and discard data. Improving elasmobranch fisheries data is of prime importance in achieving sustainably managed stocks. In both recreational and commercial fisheries, inappropriate handling of elasmobranch catches prior to release can also contribute to increased post release mortality, further undermining those management measures designed to reduce fishing mortality. For over 10 years, The Shark Trust has produced Fisheries Advisories for the fishing industry with the aims of protecting vulnerable elasmobranch species and promoting sustainable elasmobranch fisheries. The Fisheries Advisories are used in numerous sectors of the fishing industry and by multiple government agencies, in the UK and EU, and have been translated into seven languages. In order to determine their effectiveness, The Shark Trust Fishery Advisories are critically assessed using survey and interviews with various end users from within the fishing industry and fisheries regulation. Future development opportunities for the Fisheries Advisories are discussed.
6013: The endangered basking shark (Cetorhinus maximus) is experiencing pressure from fisheries, coastal development, and climate change. Yet, fundamental information about its spatio-temporal habitat use is lacking at the edges of its northern range, increasing the vulnerability to human activities. Species distribution models provide a powerful tool to investigate how environmental factors influence shark occurrence over annual and sub-annual time scales. Here, I will present preliminary results for such relationships in basking sharks along the Norwegian coast, based on observations collected as part of a national Citizen Science project called “Dugnad for havet”. In my talk, I will highlight predicted hotspots of basking shark occurrences in Norway based on a high-resolution species distribution model and discuss the potential of using citizen science observations in such models. In conjunction with in-situ tracking data, these results will allow us to investigate the co-occurrence of obtained distributional hotspots with current and future human activities and highlight areas of elevated scientific and management importance at the northern edge of the species’ distribution in the light of competing management priorities and a changing climate.
6014: Elasmobranch are characterized by specific life history traits that make them vulnerable to fishing and other anthropogenic factors. In the North Sea, rays and skates are mainly caught as bycatch, and have low commercial value. Studies are working toward defining a picture of the status of their populations and addressing the mortality inferred by fisheries. Currently population status is derived from a trend based analysis of scientific survey time series. Rajidae stocks fall in ICES category 3, including data-deficient stocks which lack analytical assessments and whose advice is given under a precautionary approach since 2012. Recently, new empirical approaches linked to life-history traits and fishing history have been developed. In this study, different approaches applied within ICES have been compared for the landings advice of thornback ray, Raja clavata. This is the main commercially important Rajidae species. Among them are the two trend-based rules “2 over 3” and “2 over 5”, currently employed for the advice of the Rajidae complex, and the empirical rules rfb and rb. This study aims at providing an overview of the implications of the main data-deficient models for the advice of Thornback ray, exploring the possibilities for conservation of Rajidae species in the North Sea.
6015: The millennial coastal exploitation by humans has modified and depleted coastal food webs throughout the globe. Coastal shark fisheries increased worldwide in the late 20th century due to global demand for shark products. In Quintana Roo, coastal environments harbored diverse and numerous coastal sharks for millennia. This interdisciplinary research documents the presence and exploitation of sharks on Holbox Island by integrating archaeological data, fishers' Local Ecological Knowledge (LEK) surveys with a spatial component, open interviews, and literature analyses. Studying LEK of top predators in islands that are contemporary touristic hotspots for global tourism and face environmental threats provides an opportunity to examine the long-term availability and exploitation of top predators as a fishery resource and as a cultural and biodiversity component. Seventy-eight LEK fishers' surveys allowed documenting over 15 shark species that were common in the Holbox region from families Carcharhinidae, Shpyrnidae, Lamnidae, and Ginglymostomatidae. Archaeological shark records also denote the high presence of shark families in the area. LEK fishers' surveys also documented the exploitation of sawfishes. The geospatial component of the survey allowed identifying 20 sites that were important for sharks near the coastal area of Holbox. Results contribute to understanding shark-human interactions through time and generate baseline knowledge that can help fisheries and biodiversity management. The above is relevant since the local economy relies on healthy coastal landscapes and biodiversity. Our methodology and results can help other Islands that face growing tourism like Holbox and have insufficient data on fishing activities and landscape biodiversity.

6016: Understanding habitat use patterns on a species-specific basis is crucial information for more effective fisheries management. In this study, we employed two techniques – stable isotopes of muscle tissue and vertebrae microchemistry – to analyze and compare the habitat use of three co-occurring species of coastal Myliobatiformes stingrays in different stages of their life cycles. We sampled a total of 37 individuals comprising Hypanus guttatus (n = 14), H. marinae (n = 11), and H. berthalutzae (n = 12). We estimated the proportional contribution of marine and estuarine sources to the diet using SIMMR, a Bayesian stable isotopic mixing model, while the vertebrae microchemistry data were analyzed through permutational analysis of variance (PERMANOVA). Overall, both analyses clearly demonstrate strong differences in habitat use between species. Both SIMMR and microchemistry results revealed that H. guttatus displays several entry and exit movements in estuarine areas, while H. marianae has a high specificity for its coral reef habitats, and the prevalent use of deeper waters (between 50 and 100 m deep) by adults of H. berthalutzae. Within species, PERMANOVA results yielded significant differences in habitat use between sexes for H. guttatus, and H. berthalutzae, while H. marianae displayed no differences between sexes or life stages. This is the first study to ever use data from stable isotopes and vertebrae microchemistry in elasmobranchs, which demonstrate to be accurate descriptors of the distinct environments these species occupy. Furthermore, they provide a more holistic understanding of the habitat use of these species across different time scales.

6017: Region specific anthropogenic impacts on whale sharks in the areas around the Galapagos and the Eastern Pacific have not yet been assessed. During the past decade we have gathered data on whale shark movements achieved through active tracking through satellite tagging and passive tracking through photo identification efforts. Between 2011-2021 we have tagged 106 whale sharks with 129 tags, 124 of which gave enough data for analysis. We have also identified 522 individuals through the global catalogue of whale sharks (sharkbook.ai). These data are helping us decipher the movement ecology of whale sharks in the region, which anthropogenic impacts affect them most, and where in the ETP they are most heavily impacted. For this purpose we are examining the impact of purse-seine fisheries, vessel strikes, and the effects of El Niño/La Niña ocean phenomena on whale shark movements as a proxy for climate change impact. Fishing and marine traffic hotspots are identified using open source AIS data and measured through spatial density analysis and spatial overlap with the movement patterns of whale sharks in the area using QGIS and R. Further connectivity and population indices are reviewed by applying models based on the lagged identification rate to the Galapagos photo-ID dataset. This study is complementary to the recent publication by Womersley et al. 2022 which analysed vessel traffic impact around the globe and identified the Eastern Pacific as the area where whale sharks had the highest overlap with fishing vessels.
6018: The Eastern Tropical Pacific (ETP) is a large expanse of ocean exceptionally rich in biodiversity with abundant sharks and other marine predators, particularly around the oceanic islands of this region. However, shark populations are declining, and little is known about their ecology, migratory movements, and spatial dynamics. Hence, our main goal was to study an apex predator in the ETP from their northernmost refuges (Marías, Revillagigedo) to their southern abodes (Galapagos). We tagged 35 tiger sharks, Galeocerdo cuvier, with coded acoustic transmitters (V16) and 13 sharks with satellite tags (SPOT), in Marías, Revillagigedo, Cocos and Galapagos islands from 2010 to 2018. Tiger sharks resided for longer periods of time and remained at the islands for weeks, months and even years, especially in the warmer months, before performing large-scale movements. Some of the large-scale movements were between the Revillagigedo and the Gulf of California, and between the Galapagos and 200 km south of Malpelo and the northern coast of Ecuador. Our results show that most tiger sharks were resident and moved over short distances within a home range of less than 100 km around different oceanic islands in the ETP, whereas few individuals moved exceptionally large distances of 2000 km or more. Such movements have strong implications in the design of protective zones around isolated oceanic islands and in the description of movement corridors for mobile apex predators in the ETP.

6019: Horizontal and vertical movements of marine organisms are reflective of habitat preference and behavioural patterns in activity. The development of electronic tags allowed studies into the migrations and movements of many marine species. However, such studies into the vertical movements of benthic predators remain understudied. In this study, blonde skates, Raja brachyura, and spotted skates, R. montagui, were tagged with CEFAS G5 ‘pop-off’ data storage tags in the North Sea and English Channel. Tagging took place on commercial and survey vessels in 2021 and 2022, and 81 individuals were tagged. As of June 2022, data from 7 tags were successfully acquired after tags were found by fishers or beachcombers. Diel vertical migrations, time-at-depth profiles and activity budgets were used to determine space-use patterns and preferences concerned with depth and temperature for mature individuals. The outcomes of this research will contribute a deeper understanding of the underlying processes that drive fish movements and distribution.

6020: Unlike reef manta rays, the movement ecology of endangered oceanic manta rays (Mobula birostris) is poorly understood. In Aotearoa New Zealand, M. birostris are known to occur off the North Island during at least the spring and summer months, but their distribution and habitat use is largely unknown. Here we provide preliminary observations on the movements and diving of M. birostris in northern New Zealand using satellite telemetry. A total of eight adult M. birostris were tagged with SPLASH10F GPS Fastloc satellite tags (n=7) and miniPAT archival satellite tags (n=1) off the northeast coast of the North Island of New Zealand in 2019 and 2021. Tagging duration ranged from 9-199 days, with minimum distances covered by each individual ranging from 249-4,447 km. Analysis of these tracks suggest that oceanic mantas off northeastern New Zealand spend the majority of their time (>84%) in surface waters (<50m depth), with occasional dives to the seafloor in 70-120m depth. Importantly, six of the tagged individuals migrated northwards out of NZ coastal waters during the month of March as water temperatures cooled, with three of them reaching Fiji or Tonga before their tags released. Of these 6 migrating individuals, five made repeated dives (2-6 dives/individual) below 1000m, which we postulate may be to aid in navigation during northward migration. Our study provides first insights into the movement ecology of M. birostris in New Zealand and suggests targeted future research directions to better understand the movements and habitat use of this important yet poorly-known endangered species.
6021: Baseline assessments provide information on species assemblages that can inform conservation actions through identifying biodiversity hotspots or investigating the influence of different environmental factors on species abundance and richness. Coiba National Park and its Special Zone of Marine Protection in Panama situated in the Eastern Tropical Pacific is a unique area of marine endemism and high biodiversity. Several studies have been conducted in the area on the assemblage and ecology of corals, cetaceans and selected shark and turtle species along with the socio-economic impacts of fisheries; however, the assemblages of sharks and rays have yet to be quantified. Using baited remote underwater videos (BRUVs), we created a baseline assessment of these two groups and investigated the influence of protection status and seasonality on species richness and abundance. Three shark species and eight ray species were observed on the BRUVs (n=203 deployments). Species abundance and richness were found to be higher within the Coiba marine protected area (MPA) compared to surveys outside of the park’s boundaries. Species abundance and richness were not found to be significantly different between the wet and dry seasons. The results from this study will help to inform conservation strategies and support greater management effectiveness in the Coiba National Park and the surrounding area. With a well-enforced and successful MPA, Coiba can not only provide an example of effective marine protection but it also has the potential to attract more tourists to the area, providing an essential economic boost post-COVID.
6022: Marine protected areas (MPAs) are regarded as a useful tool to protect elasmobranchs. However, these species are generally not a primary target when designing MPAs and how they benefit from these remains to be better understood. To this end, acoustic telemetry has shown to be a very fitting tool. The Arrábida marine park is a temperate coastal MPA off the Portuguese West coast, near two important fishing ports, Sesimbra and Setúbal. The common stingray (Dasyatis pastinaca) is a medium-sized viviparous ray found mostly in shallow waters from Norway to Senegal and the Mediterranean. This species is caught throughout its range and is currently classified as vulnerable by the IUCN. To study their space use and residency in this MPA, 28 individuals were tagged with acoustic transmitters and monitored for an average of 625 days and up to over 1000. Average residency was low (Residency Index=0.211) ranging from RI=0.002 to RI=0.588. Their presence in the marine park was markedly seasonal, highest during the coldest months and with virtually all individuals leaving during the warmer months of the year. During their absence, individuals were detected in the nearby Sado estuary, where they likely remained for reproductive purposes as suggested by the literature on Dasyatis. This pattern was repeated at least twice by seven individuals during the entire monitoring period. These results show common stingrays are not protected year-round by this marine park, which they leave during the reproductive season. We discuss additional measures that could be considered to improve their protection.

6023: Shark bycatch and depredation occurs frequently in the offshore marine parks surrounding Lord Howe Island, Australia. This causes loss of bait, fishing gear and catch for fishers and sharks can be injured or killed when bycaught. To understand this shark-fisher conflict and identify ways to mitigate it, we applied a multi-disciplinary approach including acoustic telemetry, vessel tracking, logbook data and surveys of local fisher knowledge. Galapagos sharks (Carcharhinus galapagensis) were tagged with acoustic transmitters and detected within a receiver array and charter fishing vessel activity was determined using Vessel Monitoring System data. Kernel density analyses assessed the spatial and temporal overlap between shark detections and fishing vessel presence, identifying several areas where higher fishing effort overlapped with greater shark detections, predominantly at shelf edges. Substantially higher residency values were recorded for three individuals at a location where fish waste was regularly discarded, suggesting a change in movement patterns resulting from food provision. Statistical models indicated that detection rates were higher in locations with higher fishing activity, greater bathymetric complexity and during summer. Logbook data showed a mean annual catch of 1,114 sharks with >95% released. Fishers reported methods that they currently use to reduce shark interactions, including fishing deeper than 100m, switching from rod and reel to handlines and electric reels, using jigs and lures instead of bait and rotating fishing locations. Diversifying target species also reduced shark interactions. The novel multi-disciplinary approach used in this case study should be adopted elsewhere to help characterise and manage shark-fisher conflicts.

6024: High-resolution, long-term datasets are critical in documenting ecosystem and population changes, as well as for differentiating natural changes from those caused by humans. Mobilising the resources necessary to collect such data for vulnerable shark and ray populations, however, remains a major challenge in elasmobranch conservation and research. Here, we used two low-cost, high-resolution camera rigs (MantaCams) to monitor the presence and residency of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) within a marine protected area in Seychelles, near-continuously for a year (April 2021 to April 2022). The MantaCams were set-up to capture images every ten seconds at a key manta aggregation site offshore of D’Arros Island and were sequentially deployed every few days to maximise site coverage throughout the year. The analysis of 1,326,926 MantaCam images from 133 deployments resulted in 913 sightings of 152 individuals (74 males, 76 females, 2 unknown), including the identification of 43 new mantas. MantaCams also observed nine adult females that were in various stages of pregnancy, as well as various instances of courtship behavior. To-date, the sighting records from the MantaCams comprise 34 % of all records collected since the establishment of the Seychelles Manta Ray Project in 2013, and were associated with the identification of more new individuals at this site than had been recorded in any year prior for the whole country. Collectively, this highlights the value of remote camera deployments to long-term, marine monitoring programs for vulnerable fauna that display high site fidelity.

6025: Pakistan has an important shark fisheries contribution annually about 12,000 m. tons. Although there is no aimed fishery for sharks in Pakistan but sharks are caught as bycatch of gillnet, longline and trawl fisheries. Tuna gillnet fishery is major contributor of pelagic sharks in Pakistan whereas sting rays and rhino sharks are mainly harvested through bottom-set gillnets in coastal and offshore waters. At present, wings of stingrays are exported from Pakistan to southeast Asia which is in addition to shark fins which is traditionally being exported to Hong Kong for almost two centuries. Although there are a number of laws which are enacted to manage shark in Pakistan both at federal and provincial levels. Pakistan is a signatory of the CITES Agreements and as such no sharks (or their fins) included on various appendices can be exported, however, shark fins including those in the Appendix-II are exported from Pakistan. Provincial Wildlife law of Sindh puts a blanket ban on catching sharks, however, the concerned Department has no infrastructure for the implementation on this law. In addition, Provincial Fisheries Departments have put ban on catching and marketing of CITES listed sharks and all rhino sharks, however, there is no control on catching and marketing of these species. There is no two opinions that shark resources are dwindling in Pakistan and despite adequate legislative cover, there is no effective implementation mechanism It is feared that major depletion of sharks species or even their extinction.
6026: India is one of the leading elasmobranch fishing nations which is driven by the bycatch and small-scale targeted fishing. The continuous decline in shark landing and increased demand of sea-food has instigated the demand of other chondrichthyans such as rays, guitarfishes and skates in the country. The surveys and reports of these batoids landed along the coast are based on commercially significant and conservation prior species. When batoids are extremely susceptible to population decline from overexploitation, a species-specific list of batoids exploited in the fishery is inevitable. We recorded 45 species of batoids (under genus Benthobatis, Narcine, Torpedo, Tetronarce, Narke, Dipturus, Orbiraja, Acroteriobatus, Rhinobatos, Glaucostegus, Rhynchobatus, Rhina, Gymnura, Plesiobatis, Brevitrygon, Himantura, Pateobatis, Pteroplatytrygon, Maculabatis, Urogymnus, Neotrygon, Taeniurops, Aetobatus, Rhinoptera and Mobula) from the major and minor harbours and landing centre’s along the coast of 4 leading maritime states in south Indian, irrespective of fishery value. The analysis of landing shows that batoid fishery in the country is still driven by highly threatened species. The electric rays, skates, small guitar fishes and stingrays with no fishery value are equally exploited as the bulk catch of these species with low turnover in fishery get auctioned for high amounts by the small-scale factories producing fish manure and animal feed. Consequently, the fisherman retains the non-commercial bycatch during trawling. The study draws attention towards reconsidering the fisheries regulation and conservation acts in India.
6027: Two decades ago the situation for sharks and rays in European waters was pretty grim. There were no limits for fisheries on elasmobranchs and endangered species did not have protection. Many species were in decline or had populations and historically low levels. A concerted effort by conservationist around Europe has led to a substantial increase in protective management measures aimed at improving the status of sharks and rays in EU waters, but are we there yet? Have these changes in the policy landscape yielded a significant result in the ocean? We present an overview of EU internal laws and regulations that apply to elasmobranch management with a validation of the level of change that has been achieved at a species level with an in depth analysis of several measures to pin point where the key to effective conservation of elasmobranchs lies. We differentiate between management of skates and rays, which are traditionally harvested commercially, and sharks which, with a few exceptions, tend to by bycatch species in EU fisheries. We end with clear policy recommendations and follow up actions for legislators and, who knows, maybe even a song!
6028: The shark fishery in Tanjungluar Lombok is one of the largest target shark fisheries in Indonesia. Fishers from this location mainly use surface longlines to catch pelagic sharks in the eastern Indian Ocean and adjacent waters. We used 20-year landing data to identify a possible decline in shark production due to the fishery. A daily basis catch data collection has been applied at Tanjungluar since 2014. This method provided more robust data and showed a stable catch pattern rather than using the sampling-based method applied earlier. In general, the total catch of sharks caught by the surface longline fisheries varied from around 300 individuals per month in the low season to more than 1000 individuals in the peak season. Two CITES-listed species, Carcharhinus falciformis, and Sphyrna lewini were dominant in the shark catch composition within the last two decades. The silky shark contributed around 20-60% of the total shark catch every month and showed an upward trend in the catch from 2005 to 2021. Interestingly, the implementation of either CITES mechanisms for the species or the national shark management program seemed to have no or less impact on this target fishery. We discussed some possible factors that may sustain the shark fishery.

6029: Unsustainable catches, driven in part by illegal trade, threaten 70% of the 52 shark and 85% of 71 ray species confirmed or suspected to occur in Bangladesh. Reported landings of elasmobranchs from targeted and non-targeted small-scale and industrial fisheries have declined by half from 6,234 tons over the past two decades, while official exports of dried shark fins (combined with fish maw) spiked at over 2,000 tons between 2018-2020. There is growing concern about the harmful effects of overfishing these apex predators on local livelihoods, food security, and the national economy. CITES Appendix I and II listings of globally threatened sharks and rays have catalysed efforts to improve their conservation management in Bangladesh. In 2021, the Bangladesh Wildlife Act was amended to strictly protect species assessed as Critically Endangered or Endangered in the IUCN Red List and/or listed in CITES Appendix I, and to regulate possession and trade of species assessed as Vulnerable and/or listed in CITES Appendix II. Non-Detriment Finding assessments for four species/species groups, including 15 CITES Appendix II listed species, confirmed the need for improved interagency collaboration, monitoring, and trade transparency. These NDFs also highlighted the need to reduce non-target catches and domestic consumption and trade that will not necessarily be reduced through stricter regulations on international trade. Improved prospects for conservation management of elasmobranchs initiated through collaborative research, policy development, trainings, and educational outreach exemplify how CITES listings can catalyse institutional collaboration and empower government and non-government stakeholders to implement evidence-based conservation plans.
6030: Despite being fully protected in New Zealand waters since 2011, significant gaps remain in our knowledge of nearly all aspects of the oceanic manta’s (Mobula birostris) life history and ecology in New Zealand. This lack of data has hindered comprehensive conservation management planning for this globally threatened species; New Zealand’s Department of Conservation currently lists the species as “Data Deficient” in terms of its threat classification. A focused effort to better understand the New Zealand oceanic manta population over the past four years has resulted in a significant increase in knowledge of this species’ population dynamics and habitat use. Combining citizen science and dedicated research efforts, 618 verified sightings spanning the time period of 1994 to 2022 have been collated from New Zealand waters, including 103 ventral photographic IDs, comprising 71 females, 26 males and 6 individuals of unknown sex. Furthermore, preliminary findings from intensive field work conducted in 2021-22 suggests that New Zealand supports a significant and healthy population of M. birostris. Observations include extensive feeding aggregations of more than 50 individuals, sightings of heavily pregnant females feeding alongside subadult males (disc widths of 590cm and 300cm respectively) and numerous accounts of active courtship displays. Moreover, this population shows very low incidence of injuries (17 %). These initial findings support the hypothesis that M. birostris are resident for at least part of the year in Aotearoa New Zealand and likely reproducing there and suggest that this population may be critical in global conservation efforts to recover this endangered species.

6031: The European Union and Seychelles tropical tuna purse seine fishery in the western Indian ocean incidentally captures three species of devil rays, the spinetail devil ray (Mobula mobular), the sicklefin devil ray (M. tarapacana), and the bentfin devil ray (M. thurstoni), all currently classified globally as Endangered by the International Union for the Conservation of Nature. We used observer data collected on tropical tuna purse seiners in 2010-2020 to analyse the relationship between the presence/absence of devil rays in the catches and the environmental conditions, the spatial and temporal variability of fishing locations, and fishing operational variables. We found that higher probability of capture was predicted in areas with relatively high chlorophyll-a concentrations, high sea surface temperature fronts, and low sea surface height. This may indicate that the presence of this planktivore species might be associated with mesoscale features resulting in elevated biomass of zooplankton. We also found higher probability of catching devil rays in sets on free-swimming schools of tuna than in sets on fish aggregating devices and smaller tuna catch sets. The spatial predictions identified two important areas (the Mascarene Plateau and central Indian Ridge) persistent throughout the year with higher probabilities of catching a devil ray, and two seasonal important areas (the western Arabian Sea and Equatorial Region) with higher catch probabilities during the winter monsoon regime (December-March). Information on the spatio-temporal and environmental preference of devil rays is crucial to support more holistic spatial management and conservation strategies to further reduce the bycatch of these species.

6032: Physiological processes influence the movement behavior of animals. Understanding relationships between physiology and behaviour can lead to breakthroughs in species' movement ecology but linking ephemeral physiological conditions with movement patterns has been an ongoing challenge. This is especially the case for migratory, free-roaming species notorious for displaying highly variable movement over large spatiotemporal scales. Physiological and biological variables, termed "biomarkers", can describe underlying physiological processes that influence movement, such as energy storage and utilization, growth, and development. Here, we aimed to determine the relative influence of physiology on intra-specific movement patterns of a highly migratory apex predator, the tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier). We accomplished this by analyzing 50 measured biomarkers for nutritional and energetic condition, metabolism, morphology, reproduction, and health, in addition to seasonality, on the dispersion and scale of tiger shark movement across multiple temporal periods (7 – 25 days). Overall, nutrition-related biomarkers had the largest relative influence on movement, followed by metabolic hormones, energy substrates, and morphology. Reproductive state, health, and season had negligible influence on the movement patterns observed across the temporal periods considered. These results emphasize the importance of tiger sharks acquiring, storing, and mobilizing energy to support their movements, providing important knowledge about their movement ecology. Our work presents a novel approach for addressing the challenge of linking movement patterns of free-roaming species to their physiology and has wide applicability for future studies investigating the drivers of individual variation in movement of highly mobile species.
6033: Mozambique is a hotspot for threatened and data deficient species of sharks and rays, yet a lack of site-specific information hinders the development of local and national species management plans. The largest identified population of reef manta rays (Mobula alfredi) in Africa aggregate within a 350 km upwelling zone that extends from the Bazaruto Archipelago in the north, to Zavora in the south. An 88% decline in sightings of M.alfredi along the Mozambican coastline represents one of the largest declines on record. However, Zavora (a remote and less explored bay in the region), still has consistent and frequent sightings of reef manta rays. Using sightings and photo-ID data from dive surveys conducted during 2009-2021, we investigate sightings trends, habitat preference, and population demographics of M. alfredi in Zavora Bay. Our results indicate that compared to other sites in Mozambique, abundance estimates for Zavora are still high, albeit on the decline. Our results also indicate a shift from consistent year-round sightings to a seasonal aggregation from July-November, with complete abandonment of a previously favoured cleaning station. The site and seasonal affinity of M. alfredi in Zavora Bay highlights the importance of understanding fine-scale site use within the larger home range of this population to develop local management strategies. Our findings provide evidence that Zavora Bay is a critical visitation site for reef manta rays in Mozambique and should be considered a conservation priority area for this threatened species.
6034: The sicklefin lemon shark, Negaprion acutidens, is globally understudied compared to its sister species the Atlantic lemon shark, N. brevirostris. Although it has been heavily targeted by artificial provisioning activities until 2017, its movements are still unknown in the Society Islands, French Polynesia. Here, we used acoustic telemetry to study the residency and movement patterns of the sicklefin lemon shark between June 2014 and July 2015. We deployed 21 receivers on the outer reefs of Tahiti (n=11), Moorea (n=7), and Tetiaroa (n=3), an atoll located approximately 50 km north of Tahiti and Moorea. A total of 17 mature individuals were tagged internally by ingestion or externally using a speargun. Preliminary analyses indicate that sharks were primarily detected around Moorea and at the Vallée Blanche, northeast of Tahiti, while no individuals were detected in Tetiaroa. The number of detections is higher where shark-feeding occurred during the study period and decreases with the distance from tagging location. Globally, the detections mostly occurred during the day, suggesting that adult sicklefin lemon sharks use the outer reef during the day and move to deeper waters at night. Therefore, the sicklefin lemon shark seems to be highly resident and could be impacted by artificial provisioning activities at a small spatial scale. Considering that artificial provisioning is now forbidden in French Polynesia waters, such data is crucial to understand the long-term impacts of this activity on sharks movements, and could pave the way for further studies focusing on dishabituation process regarding artificial provisioning in shark species.

6035: India is one of the leading chondrichthyan fishing nations. Most of the deep-sea chondrichthyans species are poorly known due to their low market value and low targeted sampling for research activities. In India, deep-sea chondrichthyans are caught both as targeted and bycatch, there is a lack of data on deep-sea chondrichthyans, despite their high market demand and catch. The objective of this study was to characterize the catch composition of deep-sea chondrichthyans, using extensive trawl catch data of commercial deep-sea shrimp fishery. The present paper is an attempt to provide new information on catch, integrative taxonomy, species composition current distribution, fleet size, trade and usage of deepsea chondrichthyans in India. This study based on the landing site surveys conducted during the years 2017-2021 at major fish landing centres along the west and east coast of India and Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The present findings revealed 47 species under 19 families caught in commercial and artisanal fisheries. Trawl surveys show that Cephaloscyllium silasi distribution restricted to off Kerala and South Andaman Islands of India. Hexatrygon bickelli and Squalus hemipinnis were confirmed from Kerala and Andaman Islands respectively. Highest diversity in the landings was observed at Kerala with several species recorded during the present study was new to Indian waters. Fishery was dominated by species belonging to families Echinorhinidae, Centrophoridae, and Rhinochimaeridae. Continued monitoring and collection of biological and taxonomical data from additional sources is recommended for better management measures for sustainable utilization of deep-sea chondrichthyans from Indian waters.
6036: The global trade in elasmobranch products contributes to dramatic declines in elasmobranch populations. Recognising realistic and context-appropriate solutions to mitigate trade requires a thorough grasp of elasmobranch marketplaces that are notoriously inadequate where products originate, predominantly in the global south. We assessed the market components of the elasmobranch fin trade in the Bay of Bengal, Bangladesh, using a framework designed for wildlife markets utilising mixed-method approaches. We found that markets are supply-driven and complex. Fins are supplied from protected and unprotected species, targeted and by-caught, and traded with other fishery and elasmobranch products. We highlighted challenges due to no reporting, limited monitoring and the difficulties in segregating species/products of different legal statuses. An unjust power structure between low-access harvesters and high-access actors with finances, market information and social ties was evident. The discriminative power exercising influenced unsustainable trade by high-access actors attaining excessive and unequal benefits from the market and often impacting independent decision-making of low-access actors (e.g., adopting conservation measures). We found ambiguous clarity about legality, growing distrust between fishers and fishery managers/policy-makers, and confusion regarding the infrequent seizures resulting from limited awareness, acceptance and no collaborative approach preceding law-making and enacting. These led to increased conflicts, corruption, non-compliance and unwillingness to report catch. Actors' behaviours are driven by diverse motivations, requiring a sophisticated regulation for reducing catch and trade, with local and global benefits. We provided targeted management recommendations to mitigate unsustainable trade, e.g., sustainable catch quotas, better financial arrangements, improved access to incentives for low-access actors, and other market solutions.

6037: Trade restrictions have been established to counteract the rapid global decline of sharks and rays. This has resulted from high fishing pressure, by-catch and market demand for certain products (e.g. fins). Tackling the illegal trade of endangered species poses enormous challenges for authorities, including taxonomic ambiguity, product variety, logistical issues for inspections and trade flow complexity. Traditional genetic techniques have been developed, but these techniques are either time-consuming or species-specific, and generally fail to provide a comprehensive picture of the biological complexity underlying trade patterns. Here, we explore a powerful, alternative option, based on the high-throughput sequencing of trace DNA fragments retrieved from dust and scraps left behind by trade activities. We collected 28 'shark-dust' samples from seven processing plants across Java, Indonesia, and generated shark and ray sequences through DNA metabarcoding. We also collected individual tissue samples (175) in the same processing plants and identified the species by high-throughput barcoding (HTB) for comparison. Over 74% of reads belonged to CITES-listed species i.e. hammerhead sharks (Sphyrna spp.), silky shark (Carcharhinus falciformis), bigeye thresher shark (Alopias superciliosus) and the recently CITES-listed giant guitarfish (Glaucostegus typus). A total of 75 shark and ray genera (representing half of the chondrichthyan orders) were identified, with 20 more taxa detected using the dust samples than those identified using tissue samples. Furthermore, dust samples were shown to effectively capture the species diversity being exploited. We argue that this 'shark-dust' approach is likely to become a powerful and cost-effective monitoring tool wherever elasmobranchs are traded.

6038: In the Mediterranean surface longlines (SL) the shark and ray bycatch represents around 10-15% in biomass of the total catch and the highest bycatch was found in the Alboran and Adriatic Sea. The blueshark (Prionace glauca), considered by IUCN as Critically Endangered in the Mediterranean, represent over 70% of the chondricthyan catch. In this context in South Adriatic pelagic longline fishery were tested two type of bycatch mitigation trials: circular hook and chancing fishing strategy. About the circular hook in a SL were used alternatively two type of hooks: circular (C-type), normal type (J-type). In 5 fishing days an experimental SL was used and the CPUE, bycatch-rate and %Bycatch was calculated for the C-hook and J-hook. The results showed that there were no significant differences in terms of CPUE, bycatch-rate and %bycatch between the two types of hooks. While the bluesharks caught by C-type hook showed a significantly better condition than the J-type. In the fishing strategy used by fisherman the SL fishing mostly during the night. During two consecutive fishing trips (FT) with at least 3 fishing days each, in one FT was used the standard fishing strategy (strategy 1: SL fishing mostly during the night) and in the other the reverse fishing strategy (strategy2: SL fishing mostly during the day) was used. The CPUE, bycatch-rate and %bycatch for the two fishing strategy showed that in the strategy 2 any blue shark was caught, while for the target species a significant reduction about the 30% was observed.
6039: Cocos Island is known to have one of the largest biomass levels of predatory fish in the tropics, yet our knowledge of the drivers affecting elasmobranch abundance and distribution patterns is limited. This study examined the effect of spatial, seasonal, and environmental drivers on elasmobranch assemblages at Cocos Island using baited remote underwater video stations (BRUVS) between 2016 and 2020. Elasmobranchs were detected in 95% of the BRUVS, with stations having on average 2.7 ± 1.6 species and 6.3 ± 6.5 ind/hour largely overcoming the mean relative abundance reported by BRUVS in other protected reef systems. A total of 13 species comprised the elasmobranch assemblage of Cocos Island, which was clearly divided between pelagic and benthic environments. Depth and habitat were identified as the major factors structuring elasmobranch assemblages in benthic environments, although substrate cover, distance to the coast and season were also significant predictors. Significant indicator species with stronger species-habitat associations were the silky shark Carcharhinus falciformis dominating pelagic habitats, the white tip reef shark Triaenodon obesus and the black tip reef shark Carcharhinus melanopterus dominating warm shallow areas with coral or rocky reefs, the scalloped hammerhead shark Sphyrna lewini associated with pinnacles at greater distances from the coast and the silvertip shark Carcharhinus albimarginatus with preference for deeper sandy areas in bays and inshore sites. This study represents the first attempt at describing ecological patterns of elasmobranch assemblages removing human presence from the water and using a systematic research survey in benthic and pelagic environments of Cocos Island.

6040: Information on the distribution and habitat preferences of ecologically important species is essential for their management and protection. The Avilés Canyon System (ACS) located in NE Atlantic Waters (Cantabrian Sea) was declared as Site of Community Importance (SIC) within the Nature 2000 network based on Habitat Directive 92/43/CEE. Therefore several surveys have been conducted to identify the presence of vulnerable habitats and species and to achieve a better understanding of the ecosystem function. Biomass data were gathered from two otter trawls datasets (2010 and 2011) within two different projects: LIFE+INDEMARES and ERDEM. Data were over dispersed due to the species typical spatial preferences, (a lot of zeros together with some very high values samples), thus zero-inflated GAM (Generalized Additive Models) with a negative binomial distribution were applied to predict species biomasses in the study area for the four most abundant chondricthyans: Scyliorhinus canicula, Raja clavata, Galeus melastomus, Chimaera monstrosa. A broad set of environmental variables were available to link with biomasses, but after a linear regression with a Pearson correlation test to avoid overestimation of explained variance just six environmental layers were used: depth, BPI broad, Q50 phi, S0, organic matter content (OM) of the sediments and the categorical variable bottom type. The variable that better explains their distribution is depth. The variances explained varied between 72.9% for G. melastomus and 82.6% for S. canicula. All the species studied showed a clear bathymetric distributional pattern probably linked more to feeding behavior and prey availability than to specific environmental conditions.

6041: Social and collective behaviours as well as group formation are found across the animal kingdom including sharks and rays. Animal aggregations may result from a common requirement for shared resources or favourable environmental conditions and are not necessarily driven by social attraction between individuals. In contrast, social groups rely on active social preferences between individuals. Although they have been considered mostly solitary organisms, improvements in analytical tools and the technology used to study behaviours in the wild has led to the confirmation that many elasmobranch species were more social than previously thought and to a better understanding of the form, structure, function and ecological significance of associations and grouping in sharks and rays. Here, I present some case studies I have been conducting or involved in, illustrating research on aggregations, social and collective behaviour in wild elasmobranchs. This includes species with gregarious or solitary life styles. This overview aims at presenting the latest advancements in analytical techniques (especially social network analysis) and field technology (e.g. photo-identification, acoustic telemetry, biologging, video recording or drone) used to study elasmobranch aggregating patterns and social systems, and discussing the benefits and costs of grouping and socializing in these taxa.

6042: Whale sharks (Rhincodon typus) are thought to seasonally aggregate in coastal waters to take advantage of foraging opportunities provided by enhanced localised productivity. To test this hypothesis, we examined the links between the movements of whale sharks and prey availability at Ningaloo Reef, Western Australia. In 2018, we sampled the water column using fisheries echosounder (Simrad EK60) transects and dedicated target trawls via ship-based surveys to describe the distribution, abundance and density of zooplankton prey in the vicinity of concurrently tracked whale sharks (using Fastloc-GPS tags). Using generalised additive mixed models, we examined whale shark kernel utilisation density (horizontal movement) and time-at-depth (calculated per 5 m depth bins) and (response variables) in relation to various prey measurements (n per m^3). There was a positive relationship between whale shark horizontal movement and prey density. Sharks tended to move along the 40-60 m depth contours, which were characterised by pronounced bathymetric features accumulating higher densities of prey near the seabed. However, despite shark horizontal movements centred within areas of high prey density, there was no relationship between shark time-at-depth and prey density. Sharks displayed consistent patterns of repeated descents and ascents through the water column with individuals spending ~49% of time within the upper 5 m of the water column, irrespective of vertical prey distribution. We suggest these vertical movements may reflect the difficulty of feeding on prey in the lower water column compared to filter feeding near the sea surface.

6043: Understanding the movement of highly mobile marine predators is vital for effective conservation and management. Despite being targeted in shark control programs, our knowledge of tiger shark (Galeocerdo cuvier) movement and habitat use off eastern Australia is limited. To investigate the habitat use and movements in this region, 16 sharks (157–384 cm total length) were tagged with MiniPAT pop-up satellite archival tags in 2018 and 2019. Eleven of these individuals were also fitted with satellite-linked radio transmitting tags. After release, most sharks moved off the continental shelf and travelled north, associating with seamounts as they moved toward Queensland. While at liberty, they transited through temperate, sub-tropical and tropical waters, spending the majority of time in the upper 50 m of the water column and at temperatures between 22–25 ˚C. Horizontal movement was focused in offshore waters beyond the continental slope. Increased movement over shelf waters occurred mainly during the austral spring and summer when the East Australian Current encroaches on the continental shelf. Broad latitudinal movement along the east coast of Australia was evident and highlights the connectivity between tropical and warm temperate regions.

6044: Metabolism underpins life histories, population dynamics, and extinction risk. Morphological traits that are linked to an organism's metabolism may provide a first approximation to the ecological needs to support growth, survival, and reproduction. Here we examine the relationship between respiratory physiology (i.e. gill slit height in proportion to total length) and activity level (caudal fin aspect ratio) in nearly all extant shark species (n=456). Gill slit heights and caudal fin aspect ratios were collected and measured from the field guide Sharks of the World (Ebert 2013). We used a Bayesian-phylogenetic inference model that accounts for each species' maximum size, primary habitat type, and evolutionary history. We found a strong positive relationship between gill slit height and activity level. We also show that primary habitat had a strong effect on this relationship with pelagic sharks exhibiting the highest gill slit heights and activity levels while deep water sharks showed the opposite trend. These findings suggest that proxies for metabolic demand may be available via external and easy to measure morphological traits and natural history. Insight into the metabolic demand of these animals may allow us to estimate vital life history traits that could inform ecological risk assessments.
6045: Devil rays of the genus Mobula are subject to fishing exploitation worldwide, the population's reductions are evidenced by a decline in the number of catches of these rays, for this reason, they are considered vulnerable to overexploitation. Limited biological knowledge on these species has forced the use of precautionary conservation measures in some countries where intensive fishing occurs. There is few information about the reproductive biology of these species. This study aimed to describe the reproductive activity of three endangered species of the genus Mobula (Mobula munkiana, Mobula thurstoni, and Mobula mobular) in the Gulf of California. Reproductive organs were collected during 7 years of commercial fishing (2001–2007), and data on population structure, sex ratio, gamete production, and the number of offspring per breeding period were obtained. Maturity stages were determined through histological analysis of the gonads for both sexes, and the size at maturity was estimated based on anatomical and histological characteristics of the specimens caught. According to the results, there is an urgent need to apply strict conservation measures, such as fishery closures during the breeding season (May to September) or the establishment of catch sizes after specimens have reached sexual maturity, mainly in the countries where these rays are caught.

6046: Scalloped hammerhead sharks (Sphryna lewini) routinely perform rapid deep dives to forage on meso and bathypelagic prey. These deep dives consist of intensive burst swimming followed by resting periods in the surface mixed layer. Swimming muscle temperature profiles suggest S. lewini suppress their gill function as a means to reduce convective heat loss. Such intensive swimming behavior coupled with supposedly reduced respiration raises questions concerning the aerobic and anaerobic metabolic capacity of their white swimming muscle. Measuring the activity rates of key enzymes used in aerobic and anaerobic metabolism provides an indirect indicator of the metabolic potential of a tissue. Here we measured the maximal activities of aerobic enzymes citrate synthase (CS), malate dehydrogenase (MDH) and anaerobic enzymes pyruvate kinase (PK) and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) from white swimming muscle of S. lewini and were compared to those measured from other coastal, deep-dwelling, and highly active endothermic shark species. Sphyrna lewini had significantly higher activity levels of LDH, an anaerobic enzyme, and MDH, an aerobic enzyme. Results indicate the white muscle tissue of S. lewini is highly anaerobic dependent for burst swimming but has a high potential for lactate buildup. High activity rates of MDH indicate the potential for lactate to be rapidly reduced under aerobic conditions such as those experienced in the surface mixed layer between dives. These physiological adaptations likely enable S. lewini to remain highly active while suppressing gill function during deep dives and thereby exploit a very different ecological niche from sympatric shark species.
6047: Sharks and rays support many ecological roles in coastal marine ecosystems, however widespread overfishing and habitat loss have resulted in population declines. Despite the intrinsic vulnerability of shark and ray populations due to their life-history characteristics, such as slow growth, low fecundity and late reproductive maturity, shark and ray functional community structure from a trait-based approach has rarely been quantified. Here, we provide a global assessment of shark and ray functional community structure among 230 tropical coral reefs in 42 nations across three ocean basins. We find that socio-economic conditions mediate shark and ray functional diversity, functional originality (the uniqueness of the community based on their traits) and functional dispersion (the overall breadth of trait combinations). Higher human gravity is strongly associated with degradation of all functional biodiversity metrics, while the trait structure of highly populated areas favour benthic and invertivorous sharks and rays. Large-bodied, pelagic and benthopelagic, deep diving, piscivorous and higher order carnivorous species are less abundant under increased human impacts. Biogeographically, Atlantic assemblages are more functionally original and diverse than Pacific assemblages, which are more represented by traits indicative of reef sharks rather than rays, such as fusiform body shape, ram ventilation and pelagic or benthopelagic lifestyles. Closed marine protected areas support substantially higher functional biodiversity than restricted and openly fished areas. Our findings illustrate the large-scale functional degradation of shark communities on coral reefs but identify spatial management tools as powerful avenues for protecting shark and ray functional integrity.

6048: Elasmobranchii belongs to an old evolutionary class of vertebrates that diverged 450 mya. These species present a wide diversity of reproductive strategies while preserving the ancient mode of internal fertilization. Moreover, many of them are considered endangered and may be extinct soon. Understanding the principles of sperm motility and sperm physiology is essential to developing assisted reproductive techniques for this species group. Additionally, it is also important from evolutionary and general physiological perspectives as a part of reproduction studies. Elasmobranchii species possess relatively big spermatozoa (compared to bony fishes), with an elongated spiral shape head and tail similar to one currently existing (but later diverged) in birds, reptiles, and amphibians, which can be considered an evolutionary ancient. These particular structures may be associated with the necessity to penetrate viscous ovarian fluid or the jelly layer of eggs, suggesting environmental viscosity as the driving force which shapes big-sized spermatozoa head to the spiral shape during evolution. In the present study, we observed spermatozoa motion by regular and high-speed video microscopy to visualize sperm and flagellar motion in three different Elasmobranchii species: the freshwater ray Potamotrygon motoro, the marine skate Raja asterias and the shark Scyliorhinus canicula. We investigated the effect of surrounding media viscosity on spermatozoa motility parameters and their ability to propagate, release from spermatozeugmata, and perform directional changes. Our results suggest that the surrounding media's viscosity regulates spermatozoa motility and may affect its performance during fertilization in the Elasmobranchii species.
